cards.front: Given eat(Animal) and eat(Dog), which runs for Animal a = new Dog(); eat(a);?
cards.back: eat(Animal) — the declared type wins, even though the object is a Dog
cards.extra: Overload resolution happens at compile time on the static type, so the more specific overload is not chosen. This is the classic static-binding surprise.
cards.source: baeldung.com — Static and Dynamic Binding in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Static vs Dynamic Binding
cards.example:
class Animal {}
class Dog extends Animal {}
class Ex { static void eat(Animal a) { System.out.println("Animal"); }
  static void eat(Dog d) { System.out.println("Dog"); }
  static void m() { Animal a = new Dog(); eat(a); } }

cards.front: How does the JVM implement dynamic binding?
cards.back: It looks up the method in the object's virtual table (vtable) at the call site — the same approach as C++
cards.extra: The declared type fixes the slot index; the object supplies the implementation. Exact details are JVM-specific, but the shape is that lookup.
cards.source: baeldung.com — Static and Dynamic Binding in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Static vs Dynamic Binding
cards.example:
class A { String name() { return "A"; } }
class B extends A { String name() { return "B"; } }
class Ex { static void demo() { A x = new B(); System.out.println(x.name()); } } // vtable slot -> B's method
